claim: dFB neurons appear to be a group of neurons with projections to the dorsal fan-shaped body (dFB neurons) of the central complex in the brain that serve as one output arm of the sleep homeostat in Drosophila.
source: One output arm of the sleep homeostat in Drosophila appears to be a group of neurons with projections to the dorsal fan-shaped body (dFB neurons) of the central complex in the brain.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Donlea et al., 2014; Donlea et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2016) as indicated in the Introduction section.

claim: Neurons that regulate the sleep homeostat remain poorly understood.
source: However, neurons that regulate the sleep homeostat remain poorly understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: One group of sleep-promoting upstream neurons is a set of circadian pacemaker neurons that activates dFB neurons via direct glutaminergic excitatory synaptic connections.
source: One group of the sleep-promoting upstream neurons is a set of circadian pacemaker neurons that activates dFB neurons via direct glutaminergic excitatory synaptic connections.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript including GRASP analysis, Ca2+ imaging, and RNAi experiments.

claim: A group of arousal-promoting neurons downregulates dFB axonal output with dopamine.
source: Opposing this population, a group of arousal-promoting neurons downregulates dFB axonal output with dopamine.
evidence: This claim is supported by Ca2+ imaging experiments showing dopamine reduces Ca2+ levels in dFB axonal terminals.

claim: Co-activating sleep-promoting and arousal-promoting neurons leads to frequent shifts between sleep and wake states.
source: Co-activating these two inputs leads to frequent shifts between sleep and wake states.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data showing increased sleep bout number and decreased bout length when both neuron types are activated simultaneously.

claim: dFB neurons release the neurotransmitter GABA.
source: We also show that dFB neurons release the neurotransmitter GABA and inhibit octopaminergic arousal neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAi experiments showing that knockdown of Gad1 in dFB neurons eliminates their sleep-promoting effects.

claim: dFB neurons inhibit octopaminergic arousal neurons.
source: We also show that dFB neurons release the neurotransmitter GABA and inhibit octopaminergic arousal neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by Ca2+ imaging showing that activation of dFB neurons reduces GCaMP3 fluorescence in octopaminergic neurons.

claim: dFB neurons integrate synaptic inputs from distinct sets of upstream sleep-promoting circadian clock neurons and arousal neurons.
source: We propose that dFB neurons integrate synaptic inputs from distinct sets of upstream sleep-promoting circadian clock neurons, and arousal neurons.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Sleep is regulated by dual mechanisms: the circadian clock and homeostatic drive.
source: These include dual regulation of sleep by the circadian clock and by homeostatic-drive, both of which are essential for maintaining regular sleep patterns (Allada et al., 2017; Borbély, 1982).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: dFB neurons receive inputs from Ellipsoid body R2 neurons, which encode sleep drive.
source: These dFB neurons receive inputs from Ellipsoid body R2 neurons, which encode sleep drive (Liu et al., 2016) and suppress movements stimulated by sensory cues (Donlea et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Circadian pacemaker neurons that directly synapse onto dFB neurons have not yet been reported.
source: Nevertheless, circadian pacemaker neurons that directly synapse onto dFB neurons have not yet been reported.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge prior to this study.

claim: Arousal-promoting molecules and neurons that stimulate wakefulness provide an essential balance to sleep.
source: Therefore, arousal-promoting molecules and neurons that stimulate wakefulness provide an essential balance.
evidence: This is based on logical inference about the trade-offs between sleep and wakefulness.

claim: Various arousal signals have been identified in Drosophila and their functions in promoting wakefulness are conserved in mammals.
source: In Drosophila, various arousal signals have been identified and their functions in promoting wakefulness are conserved in mammals (Crocker and Sehgal, 2008; Liu et al., 2012; Sehgal and Mignot, 2011; Ueno et al., 2012b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Arousal signals include biogenic amines (dopamine and octopamine) and neuropeptides such as Pigment Dispersing Factor (PDF).
source: These include biogenic amines (dopamine and octopamine) and neuropeptides such as Pigment Dispersing Factor (PDF) (Andretic et al., 2008; Crocker and Sehgal, 2008; Crocker et al., 2010; Parisky et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Dopamine can downregulate the activity of dFB neurons.
source: Previous studies have demonstrated that dopamine can downregulate the activity of the dFB neurons (Pimentel et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The anatomy of direct synaptic connections between dopaminergic neurons and dFB neurons is uncharacterized.
source: Nevertheless, the anatomy of direct synaptic connections between dopaminergic neurons and dFB neurons is uncharacterized.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge prior to this study.

claim: It remains unknown whether different upstream neurons that regulate the activity of dFB neurons in opposite directions synapse onto the same or distinct neurons in the dFB.
source: It remains unknown whether different upstream neurons that regulate the activity of dFB neurons in opposite directions, synapse onto the same or distinct neurons in the dFB.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge prior to this study.

claim: The behavioral consequences of simultaneous hyperactivation of sleep-promoting and wake-promoting neuronal circuits have not been investigated in animal models.
source: Moreover, the behavioral consequences of simultaneous hyperactivation of sleep-promoting and wake-promoting neuronal circuits have not been investigated in animal models.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge prior to this study.

claim: Two groups of sleep-promoting neurons form glutaminergic excitatory synaptic connections onto dFB neurons.
source: We identified two groups of sleep-promoting neurons that form glutaminergic excitatory synaptic connections onto dFB neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by GRASP analysis, Ca2+ imaging, and RNAi experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: One group of sleep-promoting neurons are circadian pacemaker neurons that express the neuropeptide Allatostatin-A (AstA).
source: One group of sleep-promoting neurons are circadian pacemaker neurons that also express the neuropeptide, Allatostatin-A (AstA), a sleep-promoting factor as well as a feeding regulator (Chen et al., 2016; Donlea et al., 2018; Hergarden et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data showing co-localization of AstA with clock proteins and by citations to prior work.

claim: Dopamine released from arousal neurons inhibits synaptic output at the axonal terminals of dFB neurons.
source: Additionally, we characterized synaptic connections from upstream dopaminergic arousal neurons onto the dFB neurons and revealed a novel wake-promoting mechanism by which dopamine released from arousal neurons inhibits synaptic output at the axonal terminals of dFB neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by Ca2+ imaging experiments showing dopamine reduces Ca2+ levels in dFB axonal terminals.

claim: dFB neurons promote sleep by releasing GABA and inhibiting octopaminergic arousal (OAA) neurons, thereby conferring long sleep bouts at night.
source: Lastly, we found that dFB neurons promote sleep by releasing GABA and inhibiting previously identified octopaminergic arousal (OAA) neurons (Crocker et al., 2010), thereby conferring long sleep bouts at night.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAi experiments and Ca2+ imaging data.

claim: dFB neurons integrate different signals reflecting the circadian clock, arousal, as well as sleep drive from distinct populations of upstream neurons.
source: Our results indicate that dFB neurons integrate different signals reflecting the circadian clock, arousal, as well as sleep drive. These signals originate from distinct populations of upstream neurons and converge on and influence the activity of common dFB neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Control flies harboring UAS-NaChBac without any Gal4 display typical sleep patterns characterized by minimal sleep at dawn and dusk (near ZT0 and ZT12, respectively), which rises to high levels during the middle of the day (near ZT6).
source: Control flies harboring UAS-NaChBac without any Gal4 display typical sleep patterns characterized by minimal sleep at dawn and dusk (near ZT0 and ZT12, respectively), which rises to high levels during the middle of the day (near ZT6; Figure 1A and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by sleep profile data shown in Figure 1A and quantified in Figure 1E.

claim: At night (ZT12—24), control flies exhibit nearly maximal levels of sleep, which is 720 min.
source: At night (ZT12—24), the control flies exhibit nearly maximal levels of sleep, which is 720 min (Figure 1A and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by sleep profile data shown in Figure 1A and quantified in Figure 1F.

claim: Hyperactivation of dFB neurons using UAS-NaChBac and the 23E10-Gal4 greatly increases daytime sleep to levels that normally occur at night.
source: Hyperactivation of dFB neurons using UAS-NaChBac and the 23E10-Gal4 (Donlea et al., 2018; Pimentel et al., 2016), which includes an enhancer from the Allatostatin-A receptor 1 (AstA-R1) gene, greatly increases daytime sleep to levels that normally occur at night (Figure 1B,D,E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by sleep profile data shown in Figure 1B, D, E, and F.

claim: Hyperactivation of neurons with UAS-NaChBac and 65D05-Gal4 phenocopied the sleep-promoting effects caused by hyperactivating dFB neurons with NaChBac.
source: Consistent with a previous report (Chen et al., 2016), we found that hyperactivation of neurons with UAS-NaChBac and 65D05-Gal4 (a Gal4 containing an enhancer from the AstA gene) phenocopied the sleep-promoting effects caused by hyperactivating dFB neurons with NaChBac (Figure 1C,D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by sleep profile data shown in Figure 1C, D, and E, and by a citation to prior work.

claim: Neuronal hyperactivation with NaChBac did not impair locomotion since the levels of activity during the wake periods were similar between the control flies and the animals expressing UAS-NaChBac.
source: The neuronal hyperactivation with NaChBac did not impair locomotion since the levels of activity during the wake periods were similar between the control flies and the animals expressing UAS-NaChBac (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by locomotor activity data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Flies that are in a sleep-like state have increased arousal thresholds similar to other animals.
source: Flies that are in a sleep-like state have increased arousal thresholds similar to other animals (Hendricks et al., 2000; Shaw et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In control flies (65D05-Gal4/+ and UAS-NaChBac/+), light stimuli caused large reductions in sleep during the 30-min period following the onset of the light stimuli.
source: In control flies (65D05-Gal4/+ and UAS-NaChBac/+), the light stimuli caused large reductions in sleep during the 30-min period following the onset of the light stimuli (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B—D).
evidence: This claim is supported by arousal data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B—D.

claim: The 65D05 > NaChBac flies did not exhibit decreased sleep (arousal) in response to the 5 min light stimulations.
source: However, the 65D05 > NaChBac flies did not exhibit decreased sleep (arousal) in response to the 5 min light stimulations (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by arousal data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and E.

claim: Hyperactivation of 65D05-Gal4 positive neurons increases sleep.
source: These data support the proposal that hyperactivation of 65D05-Gal4 positive neurons increases sleep.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the arousal experiment data.

claim: dFB neurons were proposed to secrete the AstA peptide based on AstA-positive immunostaining around the terminals of dFB neurons.
source: dFB neurons were proposed to secrete the AstA peptide based on AstA-positive immunostaining around the terminals of dFB neurons (Donlea et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The AstA-expressing neurons are most likely adjacent to rather than the dFB neurons themselves since dFB neurons are not labeled by any of the previously described AstA reporters.
source: However, the AstA-expressing neurons are most likely adjacent to rather than the dFB neurons themselves since dFB neurons are not labeled by any of the previously described AstA reporters (Chen et al., 2016; Hergarden et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is based on the observation that dFB neurons are not labeled by AstA reporters, supported by citations.

claim: dFB neurons are labeled by the 23E10-Gal4, which is an AstA-receptor (AstA-R1) reporter.
source: Rather, dFB neurons are labeled by the 23E10-Gal4, which is an AstA-receptor (AstA-R1) reporter (Jenett et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The neurons marked by AstA reporter (65D05-Gal4) function in the same sleep-promoting pathway as the dFB neurons.
source: Since hyperactivation of neurons labeled by the AstA reporter (65D05-Gal4) leads to sleep-promoting effects that are similar to those that result from hyperactivation of dFB neurons, which are labeled by the AstA-R1 reporter, we hypothesize that the neurons that are marked by AstA reporter (65D05-Gal4) function in the same sleep-promoting pathway as the dFB neurons.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the similarity of sleep-promoting effects.

claim: The AstALexA mutation eliminated anti-AstA staining in the brain.
source: As expected, the AstALexA mutation eliminated anti-AstA staining in the brain (Figure 1I and J).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1I and J.

claim: Activation of AstALexA-positive neurons (AstALexA >CsChrimson) led to an increase in daytime sleep.
source: Activation of AstALexA-positive neurons (AstALexA >CsChrimson) led to an increase in daytime sleep (Figure 1K and L).
evidence: This claim is supported by optogenetic activation data shown in Figure 1K and L.

claim: The increase in sleep due to activation of AstALexA-positive neurons was less pronounced than with the 65D05-Gal4 reporter.
source: However, the increase was less pronounced than with the 65D05-Gal4 reporter (Figure 1K and L).
evidence: This claim is supported by optogenetic activation data shown in Figure 1K and L.

claim: The 65D05-Gal4 reporter labeled several regions in the brain, including sensory processing regions such as the medulla layer of the optical lobe (med) and the primary gustatory center, the subesophageal zone (SEZ).
source: The 65D05-Gal4 reporter labeled several regions in the brain, including sensory processing regions such as the medulla layer of the optical lobe (med) and the primary gustatory center, the subesophageal zone (SEZ; Figure 2A and B), similar to previously characterized AstA-Gal4 reporter lines (AstA1-Gal4 and AstA2-Gal4) (Hergarden et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2A and B, and by a citation to prior work.

claim: The AstALexA reporter labeled many fewer neurons than the 65D05-Gal4 reporter.
source: However, the AstALexA reporter labeled many fewer neurons (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Three neurons located in the lateral posterior region of the brain were labeled by both the 65D05-Gal4 and AstALexA reporters (LPNAstA).
source: By comparing the labeling with these two reporters we found that three neurons located in the lateral posterior region of the brain were labeled by both reporters (LPNAstA; Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: The positions of LPNAstA neurons resemble a group of circadian pacemaker neurons termed lateral posterior neurons (LPNs).
source: The positions of these neurons resemble a group of circadian pacemaker neurons termed lateral posterior neurons (LPNs) (Shafer et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison with prior work on LPN positions, supported by a citation.

claim: The contributions of LPNs to sleep have not been reported previously.
source: The contributions of LPNs to sleep have not been reported previously.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge prior to this study.

claim: LPNAstA neurons express Timeless (Tim) and Period (Per), two core clock proteins expressed in Drosophila circadian pacemaker neurons.
source: We confirmed the identity of the LPNs by co-staining with Timeless (Tim; Figure 2D—F) and Period (Per; Figure 2G—I), two core clock proteins expressed in Drosophila circadian pacemaker neurons (Reddy et al., 1984; Sehgal et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2D—I and by citations to prior work.

claim: LPNAstA neurons express the AstA peptide.
source: These LPNs also express the AstA peptide and are referred to here as LPNAstA neurons (Figure 2J—L).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2J—L.

claim: LPNAstA neurons are the key AstALexA-positive neurons required for promoting sleep.
source: We tested whether LPNAstA are the key AstALexA-positive neurons required for promoting sleep by using tetanus toxin to inhibit neurotransmission from LPNAstA neurons while activating the remaining AstALexA neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by experiments using tetanus toxin to block LPNAstA neurons while activating other AstALexA neurons.

claim: The sleep-promoting effect induced in AstALexA/+ > CsChrimson flies was abolished when LPNAstA neurons were inhibited with tetanus toxin.
source: We treated these animals with red lights and found that the sleep-promoting effect induced in AstALexA/+ > CsChrimson flies was abolished (Figure 1K and L).
evidence: This claim is supported by optogenetic activation data shown in Figure 1K and L.

claim: LPNAstA neurons are sleep-promoting circadian pacemaker neurons.
source: Based on this evidence we conclude that LPNAstA neurons are sleep-promoting circadian pacemaker neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: A second group of sleep-promoting neurons are labeled by the 65D05-Gal4 but not the AstALexA reporter.
source: Because the increase in sleep caused by light activation of neurons in AstALexA/+ > CsChrimson flies was less robust than in 65D05-Gal4 > CsChrimson flies (Figure 1K and L), it is plausible that a second group of sleep-promoting neurons are labeled by the 65D05-Gal4 but not the AstALexA reporter.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the difference in sleep-promoting effects between the two reporters.

claim: Sleep-promoting effects were still observed when UAS-NaChBac was expressed under control of the 65D05-Gal4 with Gal80 expressed under control of AstALexA to inhibit Gal4 activity in LPNAstA neurons.
source: We expressed UAS-NaChBac under the control of the 65D05-Gal4, and in the same flies expressed Gal80 under the control of AstALexA to inhibit Gal4 activity in LPNAstA neurons. We still observed sleep-promoting effects in these transgenic animals including increased total daytime sleep and sleep bout length (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A—C, E—G).
evidence: This claim is supported by sleep data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A—C, E—G.

claim: The sleep-promoting effects displayed by flies with Gal80 expression in LPNAstA neurons were smaller than without the Gal80 expression.
source: The sleep-promoting effects displayed by these flies were smaller than without the Gal80 expression in LPNAstA neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D—G).
evidence: This claim is supported by sleep data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D—G.

claim: LPNAstA and additional neurons marked by the 65D05-Gal4 reporter promote sleep.
source: Together, these findings support the model that LPNAstA and additional neurons marked by the 65D05-Gal4 reporter promote sleep.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Neurons located in the superior lateral protocerebrum (SLP) were stained positive by mCherry only in flies exhibiting an increase in sleep.
source: In contrast, we found that neurons located in the superior lateral protocerebrum (SLP) were stained positive by mCherry only in flies exhibiting an increase in sleep (Figure 3—figure supplement 1I and J).
evidence: This claim is supported by FlpOut analysis data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1I and J.

claim: SLPAstA neurons are a second group of sleep-promoting neurons labeled by 65D05-Gal4.
source: These data indicate that SLPAstA neurons are a second group of sleep-promoting neurons labeled by 65D05-Gal4.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the FlpOut analysis.

claim: Neuronal activity in the dFB is required for LPNAstA and SLPAstA neurons to promote sleep.
source: Next, we tested if neuronal activity in the dFB was required for LPNAstA and SLPAstA neurons to promote sleep.
evidence: This claim is tested by experiments blocking dFB neuron activity while activating LPNAstA and SLPAstA neurons.

claim: Red light induced an increase in daytime sleep and consolidated daytime sleep into longer bouts when LPNAstA and SLPAstA neurons were activated with CsChrimson.
source: As expected, red light induced an increase in daytime sleep and consolidated daytime sleep into longer bouts (Figure 3A—F).
evidence: This claim is supported by optogenetic activation data shown in Figure 3A—F.

claim: When neurotransmission from dFB neurons was blocked with TNT, optogenetic activation of LPNAstA and SLPAstA neurons no longer promoted sleep or sleep bout consolidation.
source: However, when we blocked neurotransmission from dFB neurons with TNT (23E10-Gal4 and UAS-TNT), optogenetic activation of LPNAstA and SLPAstA neurons no longer promoted sleep or sleep bout consolidation (Figure 3A—F).
evidence: This claim is supported by optogenetic activation data shown in Figure 3A—F.

claim: Two groups of neurons promote sleep and appear to function presynaptic to dFB neurons.
source: Taken together, we identified two groups of neurons, which promote sleep and appear to function presynaptic to dFB neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: One of the groups of neurons are bona fide circadian pacemaker neurons, suggesting a direct neuronal pathway through which the circadian system regulates the sleep homeostat.
source: The finding that one of the groups of neurons are bona fide circadian pacemaker neurons suggests a direct neuronal pathway through which the circadian system regulates the sleep homeostat.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the identification of LPNAstA neurons as circadian pacemaker neurons.

claim: Both SLPAstA and LPNAstA reporters showed innervation in the SMP region.
source: Both reporters showed innervation in the SMP. The scale bar represents 20 µm. (H) Anti-tdTomato (magenta) and anti-GFP (green) staining of a whole-mount brain expressing tdTomato in dFB neurons and GFP in LPNAstA neurons (AstALexA >GFP). Both reporters stained the SMP region.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3G and H.

claim: GRASP signals were detected in the SMP region of the brain where LPNAstA, SLPAstA and dFB neurons send their projections.
source: Consistent with our double-labeling experiments (Figure 3G and H), we detected GFP fluorescence in the SMP region of the brain where LPNAstA, SLPAstA (expressing 65D05-Gal4 > UAS-mCD4-GFP1-10) and dFB neurons (expressing 23E10-LexA > lexAOp-mCD4-GFP11) send their projections (Figure 3J, Figure 3—figure supplement 1K and L).
evidence: This claim is supported by GRASP analysis data shown in Figure 3J and Figure 3—figure supplement 1K and L.

claim: After applying ATP to activate the SLPAstA and LPNAstA neurons, there was a significant increase in GCaMP3 fluorescence in dFB neurons relative to applying the imaging buffer only.
source: After applying ATP to activate the SLPAstA and LPNAstA neurons, there was a significant increase in GCaMP3 fluorescence in dFB neurons relative to applying the imaging buffer only (Figure 3K and L).
evidence: This claim is supported by Ca2+ imaging data shown in Figure 3K and L.

claim: Sleep-promoting excitatory synaptic connections exist from LPNAstA and SLPAstA neurons to the downstream dFB neurons.
source: Based on the results described above we propose the existence of sleep-promoting excitatory synaptic connections from LPNAstA and SLPAstA neurons to the downstream dFB neurons.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings.

claim: The increase in sleep due to hyperactivation by NaChBac (65D05 > NaChBac) was reduced when RNAi was directed against VGlut.
source: We found that the increase in sleep due to hyperactivation by NaChBac (65D05 > NaChBac) was reduced when RNAi was directed against VGlut—the transporter required for packaging glutamate in synaptic vesicles (Figure 4A and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by sleep data shown in Figure 4A and F.

claim: The elevation in sleep induced by NaChBac was not affected when RNAi was used to knockdown genes required for the synthesis or packaging of acetylcholine (ChAT), γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA; Gad1) and biogenic amines (VMAT).
source: In contrast, the elevation in sleep induced by NaChBac was not affected when we used RNAi to knockdown genes required for the synthesis or packaging of other major neurotransmitters including acetylcholine (ChAT), γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA; Gad1) and biogenic amines (VMAT) (Figure 4B—F).
evidence: This claim is supported by sleep data shown in Figure 4B—F.

claim: Glutamate plays an important role in conferring the sleep-promoting contributions of LPNAstA and SLPAstA neurons.
source: These observations suggest an important role for glutamate in conferring the sleep-promoting contributions of LPNAstA and SLPAstA neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the RNAi experiments.

claim: Addition of glutamate caused an increase in GCaMP6f fluorescence in dFB neurons.
source: We found that addition of glutamate caused an increase in GCaMP6f fluorescence (Figure 4G and H).
evidence: This claim is supported by Ca2+ imaging data shown in Figure 4G and H.

claim: dFB neurons did not respond to acetylcholine.
source: In contrast, these neurons did not respond to acetylcholine—another major excitatory neurotransmitter in the Drosophila brain (Figure 4I and J).
evidence: This claim is supported by Ca2+ imaging data shown in Figure 4I and J.

claim: The central clock in LPNAstA neurons contributes to the sleep promoting function of these neurons.
source: We found that the sleep-promoting effect of neuronal hyperactivation of LPNAstA neurons (65D05-Gal4 > NaChBac) during the daytime was reduced by expression of Clk∆ (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and B). This indicates that the central clock in LPNAstA neurons contributes to the sleep promoting function of these neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by sleep data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: The AstALexA mutation significantly decreased the sleep-promoting effect caused by expression of NaChBac in LPNAstA neurons.
source: We found that the AstALexA mutation significantly decreased the sleep-promoting effect caused by expression of NaChBac (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by sleep data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C and D.

claim: In addition to glutamate, AstA also contributes to the sleep-promoting function of LPNAstA neurons.
source: These results indicate that in addition to glutamate (Figure 4A) AstA also contributes to the sleep-promoting function of LPNAstA neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the AstALexA mutation experiments.

claim: Dopamine is released by tyrosine hydroxylase (TH)-expressing neurons and is an arousal-promoting molecule.
source: Dopamine is released by tyrosine hydroxylase (TH)-expressing neurons and is an arousal-promoting molecule (Liu et al., 2012; Pimentel et al., 2016; Ueno et al., 2012b), which inhibits the activity of dFB neurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work and by Ca2+ imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: The DAA neurons project to two layers within the FB: the dorsal FB layer (dFB) and the ventral FB layer (vFB).
source: We found that the DAA neurons project to two layers within the FB: the dorsal FB layer (dFB) and the ventral FB layer (vFB; Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The dorsal layer innervation of DAA neurons overlapped with the projections from dFB neurons.
source: The dorsal layer innervation of DAA neurons overlapped with the projections from dFB neurons (Figure 5B), suggesting possible synaptic connection between DAA and dFB neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: GRASP signals were observed in regions of the brain containing dFB neuronal projections, including the SMP region and the dFB.
source: We observed GRASP signals in regions of the brain containing dFB neuronal projections, including the SMP region and the dFB (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by GRASP analysis data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: After applying ATP to activate DAA neurons, there was a significant reduction in GCaMP3 fluorescence in dFB neurons relative to the effect of applying the imaging buffer only.
source: After applying ATP, we observed a significant reduction (p < 0.01, unpaired Student's t-test) in GCaMP3 fluorescence relative to the effect of applying the imaging buffer only (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by Ca2+ imaging data shown in Figure 5D and E.

claim: LPNAstA and SLPAstA sleep promoting neurons only synapse onto the SMP projections of dFB neurons, while DAA arousal neurons synapse onto both the SMP projections and the dorsal layer projections of dFB neurons.
source: While LPNAstA and SLPAstA sleep promoting neurons only synapse onto the SMP projections of dFB neurons, DAA arousal neurons synapse onto both the SMP projections and the dorsal layer projections of dFB neurons (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the immunostaining and GRASP data, illustrated in Figure 5F.

claim: SMP projections of dFB neurons were more intensively marked by DenMark, while the dorsal layer projections of dFB neurons were more heavily labeled with syt::eGFP.
source: We found that SMP projections of dFB neurons were more intensively marked by DenMark, while the dorsal layer projections of dFB neurons were more heavily labeled with syt::eGFP (Figure 5G and H).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5G and H.

claim: dFB neurons receive upstream inputs mainly through synapses in the SMP area stemming from sleep-promoting LPNAstA and SLPAstA neurons.
source: Therefore, we propose that dFB neurons receive upstream inputs mainly through synapses in the SMP area stemming from sleep-promoting LPNAstA and SLPAstA neurons.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the dendritic and axonal marker data.

claim: dFB neurons transmit signals through axonal terminals located in the dorsal FB layer.
source: Furthermore, these data suggest that the dFB neurons transmit signals through axonal terminals located in the dorsal FB layer.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the dendritic and axonal marker data.

claim: Dopamine suppresses Ca2+ dynamics in axonal terminals of dFB neurons located in the dorsal layer.
source: One possible role of the synaptic connections from DAA neurons to the axonal terminals of dFB neurons is pre-synaptic regulation of dFB neuronal output. Therefore, we asked if dopamine suppresses Ca2+ dynamics in axonal terminals of dFB neurons located in the dorsal layer, thereby negatively regulating the output from dFB neurons.
evidence: This is a hypothesis tested by Ca2+ imaging experiments.

claim: When dopamine was applied to the bath, there was a reduction in Ca2+ levels in the axonal terminals of the dFB neurons.
source: When we applied dopamine to the bath, we observed a reduction in Ca2+levels in the axonal terminals of the dFB neurons (Figure 5I and J).
evidence: This claim is supported by Ca2+ imaging data shown in Figure 5I and J.

claim: Application of either octopamine or tyramine did not change the Ca2+ dynamics in dFB neurons.
source: In contrast, application of either of two other major invertebrate biogenic amines (octopamine and tyramine) did not change the Ca2+dynamics in dFB neurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: This claim is supported by Ca2+ imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1I.

claim: Activating DAA neurons (TH-Gal4 >NaChBac) led to a drastic reduction in total sleep time (158 ± 37 min), relative to the controls (849 ± 32 min for UAS-NaChBac/+ and 982 ± 38 for TH-Gal4/+).
source: Activating DAA neurons (TH-Gal4 >NaChBac) led to a drastic reduction in total sleep time (158 ± 37 min), relative to the controls (849 ± 32 min for UAS-NaChBac/+and 982 ± 38 forTH-Gal4/+; Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by sleep data shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: Activating 65D05-Gal4 positive neurons (LPNAstA and SLPAstA) promotes sleep (1343 ± 36 min).
source: As described above, activating 65D05-Gal4 positive neurons (LPNAstA and SLPAstA) promotes sleep (1343 ± 36 min; Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by sleep data shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: Co-activating DAA and LPNAstA/SLPAstA neurons with NaChBac led to a level of total sleep time (881 ± 46 min) similar to the control flies.
source: Of significance, co-activating DAA and LPNAstA/SLPAstA neurons with NaChBac led to a level of total sleep time (881 ± 46 min) similar to the control flies (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by sleep data shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: When only the 65D05-Gal4 was used to express NaChBac, daytime sleep bouts were significantly lengthened.
source: When we only used the 65D05-Gal4 to express NaChBac, daytime sleep bouts were significantly lengthened (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by sleep bout length data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Activating DAA neurons (TH >NaChBac) resulted in fragmented sleep with a significantly reduced sleep bout length, which was most obvious for nighttime sleep.
source: Conversely, activating DAA neurons (TH >NaChBac) resulted in fragmented sleep with a significantly reduced sleep bout length, which was most obvious for nighttime sleep (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by sleep bout length data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: When LPNAstA/SLPAstA and DAA neurons were simultaneously activated, the sleep bouts were shorter than those exhibited by the control but were comparable to flies in which only the DAA neurons were activated (TH >NaChBac).
source: When we simultaneously activated LPNAstA/SLPAstA and DAA neurons with the 65D05-Gal4 and TH-Gal4, respectively, the sleep bouts were shorter than those exhibited by the control but were comparable to flies in which only the DAA neurons were activated (TH >NaChBac; Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by sleep bout length data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Activating both LPNAstA/SLPAstA and DAA neurons caused the flies to initiate many more sleep episodes, as indicated by a significant increase in the sleep bout number.
source: Additionally, activating both LPNAstA/SLPAstA and DAA neurons caused the flies to initiate many more sleep episodes, as indicated by a significant increase in the sleep bout number (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by sleep bout number data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: In control flies, wake bout length is much longer during the day than night.
source: In control flies, wake bout length is much longer during the day than night (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by wake bout length data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Activating sleep-promoting LPNAstA/SLPAstA neurons (65D05-Gal4 > NaChBac) led to a reduction in the bout length of daytime wakefulness.
source: Activating sleep-promoting LPNAstA/SLPAstA neurons (65D05-Gal4 > NaChBac) led to a reduction in the bout length of daytime wakefulness, while activating arousal-promoting DAA neurons increased the bout length of nighttime wakefulness (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by wake bout length data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Activating arousal-promoting DAA neurons increased the bout length of nighttime wakefulness.
source: Activating sleep-promoting LPNAstA/SLPAstA neurons (65D05-Gal4 > NaChBac) led to a reduction in the bout length of daytime wakefulness, while activating arousal-promoting DAA neurons increased the bout length of nighttime wakefulness (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by wake bout length data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: When the two groups of neurons were activated simultaneously, both daytime and nighttime activities were fragmented.
source: Remarkably, when the two groups of neurons were activated simultaneously, both daytime and nighttime activities were fragmented (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by wake bout length data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Thermoactivation of dFB neurons with TRPA1 (23E10 > trpA1) enhances sleep.
source: Thermoactivation of dFB neurons with TRPA1 (23E10 > trpA1) enhances sleep (Figure 7A, B, D—F).
evidence: This claim is supported by sleep data shown in Figure 7A, B, D—F.

claim: The sleep-promoting effect of TRPA1-induced activation of dFB neurons was eliminated when Gad1 was knocked down in dFB neurons using RNAi.
source: However, this effect was eliminated when we used RNAi to knockdown Gad1 in dFB neurons (23E10 > trpA1 and Gad1 RNAi; Figure 7C, D and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by sleep data shown in Figure 7C, D, and G.

claim: Significant sleep-promoting effects resulting from TRPA1-induced activation of dFB neurons were still observed when RNAi was used to suppress production of other major neurotransmitters.
source: In contrast, we still observed significant sleep-promoting effects resulting from TRPA1-induced activation of dFB neurons when we used RNAi to suppress production of other major neurotransmitters (Figure 7H—J).
evidence: This claim is supported by sleep data shown in Figure 7H—J.

claim: GABA is a necessary sleep-enhancing neurotransmitter synthesized in dFB neurons.
source: These results suggest that GABA is a necessary sleep-enhancing neurotransmitter synthesized in dFB neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the RNAi experiments.

claim: dFB neurons communicate through inhibitory neurotransmitters and express the vesicular GABA transporter.
source: This observation is in consistent with a previous report that dFB neurons communicate through inhibitory neurotransmitters and express the vesicular GABA transporter (Donlea et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Nighttime sleep is reduced upon feeding flies octopamine (OA).
source: Octopamine (OA) appears to increase wakefulness as nighttime sleep is reduced upon feeding flies OA (Crocker and Sehgal, 2008) or by activating tyrosine decarboxylase 2 (TDC2)-expressing neurons with NaChBac (tdc2-Gal4 > NaChBac) (Crocker et al., 2010) (Figure 8A).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work and by sleep data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Activating tyrosine decarboxylase 2 (TDC2)-expressing neurons with NaChBac (tdc2-Gal4 > NaChBac) reduces nighttime sleep.
source: Octopamine (OA) appears to increase wakefulness as nighttime sleep is reduced upon feeding flies OA (Crocker and Sehgal, 2008) or by activating tyrosine decarboxylase 2 (TDC2)-expressing neurons with NaChBac (tdc2-Gal4 > NaChBac) (Crocker et al., 2010) (Figure 8A).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work and by sleep data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Nighttime sleep in tdc2-Gal4 > NaChBac flies is fragmented as the number of sleep bouts increases dramatically, and the average length of each nighttime sleep bout is reduced greatly.
source: Nighttime sleep in tdc2-Gal4 > NaChBac flies is fragmented as the number of sleep bouts increases dramatically, and the average length of each nighttime sleep bout is reduced greatly (Figure 8B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by sleep bout data shown in Figure 8B and C.

claim: The tdc2-Gal4 reporter labeled neurons that project to multiple layers of the FB, including the dorsal layer where dFB neurons also project.
source: The tdc2-Gal4 reporter labeled neurons that project to multiple layers of the FB, including the dorsal layer where dFB neurons also project (Figure 8D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Most of the OA neuronal projections in the dFB were axonal (syt::eGFP).
source: Most of the OA neuronal projections in the dFB were axonal (syt::eGFP; Figure 8E).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 8E.

claim: There was a single dendritic layer in the dFB labeled with DenMark.
source: In addition, there was a single dendritic layer in the dFB labeled with DenMark (Figure 8E).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 8E.

claim: The OA neurons, which express the Tdc2-Gal4, form close connections with the dFB axonal terminals, which express 23E10.
source: Of note, the OA neurons, which express the Tdc2-Gal4, form close connections with the dFB axonal terminals, which express 23E10 (Figure 8F).
evidence: This claim is supported by GRASP analysis data shown in Figure 8F.

claim: After applying ATP to activate dFB neurons expressing P2X2, there was a dramatic reduction in GCaMP3 fluorescence in OAA neurons.
source: After applying ATP we observed a dramatic reduction in GCaMP3 fluorescence (Figure 8G and H).
evidence: This claim is supported by Ca2+ imaging data shown in Figure 8G and H.

claim: dFB sleep-promoting neurons inhibit OAA neurons.
source: These data indicate that dFB sleep-promoting neurons inhibit OAA neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the Ca2+ imaging data.

claim: A regular sleep pattern is achieved through coordinated action of neuronal signals reflecting internal sleep needs, the circadian clock and the level of arousal.
source: A regular sleep pattern is achieved through coordinated action of neuronal signals reflecting internal sleep needs, the circadian clock and the level of arousal.
evidence: This is a general statement about sleep regulation based on established knowledge.

claim: Neurons projecting to the dorsal fan-shaped body of the central complex (dFB neurons) are proposed to be the effectors of the sleep homeostat.
source: In Drosophila, neurons projecting to the dorsal fan-shaped body of the central complex (dFB neurons) are proposed to be the effectors of the sleep homeostat (Donlea et al., 2014; Donlea et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2016; Pimentel et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Multiple sleep and arousal-promoting neurons regulate the activity of dFB neurons through direct synaptic connections onto either their dendritic or axonal terminals.
source: In our study, we identified multiple sleep and arousal-promoting neurons, which regulate the activity of dFB neurons through direct synaptic connections onto either their dendritic or axonal terminals.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: LPNAstA are key neurons that provide circadian input to the dFB to influence sleep.
source: One of two groups of sleep-promoting neurons is a set of circadian pacemaker neurons, referred to as LPNAstA neurons. Thus, we propose that LPNAstA are key neurons that provide circadian input to the dFB to influence sleep.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings.

claim: Artificial co-activation of sleep and arousal-promoting neurons lead to frequent shifts between sleep and wake states.
source: Moreover, we found that artificial co-activation of sleep and arousal-promoting neurons lead to frequent shifts between sleep and wake states, indicating that temporal segregation of the activities of these regulatory neurons is necessary to maintain consolidated sleep.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the behavioral data from co-activation experiments.

claim: Temporal segregation of the activities of sleep and arousal regulatory neurons is necessary to maintain consolidated sleep.
source: Moreover, we found that artificial co-activation of sleep and arousal-promoting neurons lead to frequent shifts between sleep and wake states, indicating that temporal segregation of the activities of these regulatory neurons is necessary to maintain consolidated sleep.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the behavioral data from co-activation experiments.

claim: The NMDA receptor is proposed to promote sleep in Drosophila.
source: The NMDA receptor is proposed to promote sleep in Drosophila (Robinson et al., 2016; Tomita et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The identity of the sleep-promoting glutaminergic synapse was unclear prior to this study.
source: Yet, the identity of the sleep-promoting glutaminergic synapse was unclear.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge prior to this study.

claim: Axons extending from both sets of sleep-promoting neurons (LPNAstA and SLPAstA) form close associations with dendrites of dFB neurons in the SMP region.
source: Using the GRASP technique, we found that axons extending from both sets of sleep-promoting neurons (LPNAstA and SLPAstA) form close associations with dendrites of dFB neurons in the SMP region.
evidence: This claim is supported by GRASP analysis data.

claim: Glutamate is required in the LPNAstA and SLPAstA neurons to promote sleep and activate dFB neurons.
source: Furthermore, we demonstrated that glutamate is required in the LPNAstA and SLPAstA neurons to promote sleep and activate dFB neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAi experiments and Ca2+ imaging data.

claim: ATP activation of LPNAstA and SLPAstA neurons expressing the P2X2 channel led to increased activity of dFB neurons.
source: We used ATP to activate LPNAstA and SLPAstA neurons expressing the P2X2 channel and found that this manipulation lead to increased activity of dFB neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by Ca2+ imaging data.

claim: The combination of GRASP and activity data suggest the existence of glutaminergic synapses between LPNAstA/SLPAstA and dFB neurons.
source: The combination of these GRASP and activity data suggest the existence of glutaminergic synapses between LPNAstA/SLPAstA and dFB neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the GRASP and Ca2+ imaging data.

claim: The LPN circadian pacemaker neurons express AstA—a neuropeptide, which has been linked to sleep promotion.
source: We found that the LPN circadian pacemaker neurons express AstA—a neuropeptide, which has been linked to sleep promotion (Chen et al., 2016; Donlea et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data and citations to prior work.

claim: AstA released by LPNAstA and/or SLPAstA function as a sleep-promoting signal.
source: Our observations suggest that AstA released by LPNAstA and/or SLPAstA function as a sleep-promoting signal.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings.

claim: AstA released by LPNAstA and/or SLPAstA neurons might act directly on the AstAR1 in dFB neurons.
source: Because dFB neurons are labeled by an Allatostatin-A Receptor 1 (AstAR1) reporter, the AstA released by LPNAstA and/or SLPAstA neurons might act directly on the AstAR1 in dFB neurons. This possibility is supported by our GRASP analyses indicating that LPNAstA/SLPAstA and dFB neurons are in close contact.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the GRASP data and the expression of AstAR1 in dFB neurons.

claim: AstAR1 has a role in promoting sleep.
source: AstAR1 has a role in promoting sleep (Donlea et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Dopamine is an arousal neuromodulator in both fruit flies and mammals.
source: Dopamine is an arousal neuromodulator in both fruit flies and mammals (Andretic et al., 2008; Herrera-Solis et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2012; Ueno et al., 2012a; Ueno et al., 2012b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In flies, dopamine can switch dFB neurons from an active to a quiescent state.
source: In flies, dopamine can switch dFB neurons from an active to a quiescent state (Pimentel et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: A novel synaptic basis for dopaminergic regulation of dFB neurons was revealed in this study.
source: In our study, we revealed a novel synaptic basis for dopaminergic regulation of dFB neurons.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Dopaminergic arousal neurons (DAA) form close associations at various locations along the dendritic and axonal regions of dFB neurons.
source: Our GRASP analyses reveal that dopaminergic arousal neurons (DAA) form close associations at various locations along the dendritic and axonal regions of dFB neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by GRASP analysis data.

claim: DAA neurons form synapses with axons of dFB neurons in the dFB region.
source: In addition, based on staining of dendritic and axonal makers, we propose that DAA neurons also form synapses with axons of dFB neurons in the dFB region.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the immunostaining data.

claim: Dopamine contributes to arousal by suppressing the synaptic output from sleep promoting dFB neurons.
source: Thus, we propose that dopamine also contributes to arousal by suppressing the synaptic output from sleep promoting dFB neurons.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the Ca2+ imaging data showing dopamine reduces Ca2+ levels in dFB axonal terminals.

claim: dFB neurons receive both sleep-promoting glutaminergic and arousal-promoting dopaminergic inputs.
source: dFB neurons receive both sleep-promoting glutaminergic and arousal-promoting dopaminergic inputs.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Simultaneous activation of sleep-promoting and arousal-promoting inputs by expressing UAS-NaChBac under control of the TH-Gal4 and 65D05-Gal4 lines cause the flies to rapidly shift between sleep and wake states.
source: Moreover, simultaneous activation of these opposing inputs by expressing UAS-NaChBac under control of the TH-Gal4 and 65D05-Gal4 lines cause the flies to rapidly shift between sleep and wake states.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from co-activation experiments.

claim: Flies with simultaneous activation of sleep-promoting and arousal-promoting neurons are unable to experience long sleep bouts at night or stay awake for long periods during the day.
source: Consequently, the animals are unable to experience long sleep bouts at night or stay awake for long periods during the day.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from co-activation experiments.

claim: These observations argue for a requirement for temporal segregation of input from sleep-promoting LPNAstA and SLPAstA neurons, and the arousal-promoting DAA neurons.
source: These observations argue for a requirement for temporal segregation of input from sleep-promoting LPNAstA and SLPAstA neurons, and the arousal-promoting DAA neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the behavioral data from co-activation experiments.

claim: GABA is an inhibitory neurotransmitter and is known to promote sleep in flies and mammals.
source: GABA is an inhibitory neurotransmitter and is known to promote sleep in flies and mammals (Agosto et al., 2008; Chung et al., 2017; Jones, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: dFB neurons use GABA as their sleep-promoting neurotransmitter.
source: We found that dFB neurons use GABA as their sleep-promoting neurotransmitter and that one of the downstream targets for dFB neurons are octopaminergic arousal-promoting (OAA) neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAi experiments showing that knockdown of Gad1 in dFB neurons eliminates their sleep-promoting effects.

claim: One of the downstream targets for dFB neurons are octopaminergic arousal-promoting (OAA) neurons.
source: We found that dFB neurons use GABA as their sleep-promoting neurotransmitter and that one of the downstream targets for dFB neurons are octopaminergic arousal-promoting (OAA) neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by GRASP analysis and Ca2+ imaging data.

claim: dFB neurons and OAA neurons form synapses.
source: Based on GRASP analysis, we suggest that dFB neurons and OAA neurons form synapses.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the GRASP analysis data.

claim: Activating dFB neurons inhibits OAA neurons, which may serve to maintain long sleep bouts at night.
source: Because activating dFB neurons inhibits OAA neurons this inhibitory effect may serve to maintain long sleep bouts at night, since hyperactivation of OAA neurons causes fragmentation of nighttime sleep.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the Ca2+ imaging data and the behavioral effects of activating OAA neurons.

claim: Hyperactivation of OAA neurons causes fragmentation of nighttime sleep.
source: Because activating dFB neurons inhibits OAA neurons this inhibitory effect may serve to maintain long sleep bouts at night, since hyperactivation of OAA neurons causes fragmentation of nighttime sleep.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data showing increased sleep bout number and decreased bout length when OAA neurons are activated.

claim: Activation of dFB neurons inhibits the dopaminergic neurons that project to the mushroom bodies.
source: Activation of dFB neurons inhibits the dopaminergic neurons that project to the mushroom bodies (Berry et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: This inhibition of dopaminergic neurons that project to the mushroom bodies was proposed to impair forgetting.
source: This inhibition was proposed to impair forgetting.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The dFB region is part of the central complex, which integrates multiple types of sensory information.
source: Finally, given that the dFB region is part of the central complex, which integrates multiple types of sensory information (Wolff et al., 2015), we propose that the GABA released by dFB neurons may provide inhibitory modulation that increases the threshold for sensory responses in sleeping animals.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: GABA released by dFB neurons may provide inhibitory modulation that increases the threshold for sensory responses in sleeping animals.
source: Finally, given that the dFB region is part of the central complex, which integrates multiple types of sensory information (Wolff et al., 2015), we propose that the GABA released by dFB neurons may provide inhibitory modulation that increases the threshold for sensory responses in sleeping animals.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the role of the central complex and the finding that dFB neurons release GABA.
